clue.text: How serviceman ends up with uncertain rank …

indicators.note: ends calls for the final letter of the word serviceman

parts.note: uncertain means doubtful, which is iffy in informal speech

explanation.surface: A soldier's career leaves him with a doubtful position in the hierarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 4 Across. 'rank' looks like a military grade but is the adjective for a foul smell; the answer is British slang for smelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Rank as an adjective describes a strong, offensive odour, and this British slang word means smelly.

clue.text: Can't help clear man with problems coming up inside

indicators.note: inside means the following pieces are put within the word for clear

parts.note: net means clear, as in net profit after deductions
Ed is a man's name

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the word for problems is read from bottom to top

parts.note: sums are arithmetic problems

explanation.surface: Someone unable to assist a worker whose troubles keep mounting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clear' means net as in net profit, after deductions. 'coming up' reverses only because this is a down clue, read from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says necessity compels, so one has no choice about doing something.

clue.text: Bloomer said to make a meal

indicators.note: said signals that the word for a bloomer is taken by its sound

parts.note: a bloomer is a plant that blooms, a blossom

explanation.surface: A bloomer loaf is reported to be enough for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is also a British loaf of bread, which makes the surface sound like baking.
explanation.definitionFit: Meal is coarsely ground grain, close kin to finely milled wheat powder.

clue.text: Teenager Tony urges reform

indicators.note: reform means the letters of Tony urges are made into a new shape

explanation.surface: An adolescent called Tony is pushing for change.
explanation.definitionFit: A young person, a child or adolescent.

clue.text: … and is charged to keep going

definitions.text: … and is charged to keep going

parts.words: … and is charged to keep going
parts.note: read on from the serviceman of 1 Across: a trooper who is on a charge for misconduct, and also the idiom for carrying on through hardship

explanation.surface: Continuing the first clue, the serviceman is put on a charge yet must persevere.
explanation.definitionFit: To persevere doggedly in spite of difficulty, as a trooper marches on regardless.

clue.text: Sort coins — shillings

parts.note: specie is money in the form of coins
s is the abbreviation for shillings in old British money

explanation.surface: Someone separating coins from shillings.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort or kind is a type, as in a class of living things.

clue.text: I carry pounds around — that's an understatement

indicators.note: around means the word for pounds goes round the next pieces

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, doubled to show the plural
to tote is to carry

explanation.surface: Saying I lug heavy weights about is putting it mildly.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech that says less than it means, often by denying the opposite, as in 'not bad'.

clue.text: Offspring is a girl

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A child is described as being a daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: In law and genealogy the word means children or descendants.

clue.text: Sport one race's undoing

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a sport
one is the Roman numeral I
a race in the sense of a people, a nation

explanation.surface: Losing a single race brought about one team's downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Undoing means downfall, utter destruction.

clue.text: Time to hand on the trust at last

parts.note: to hand means close by, which is nigh

indicators.note: at last asks for the final letter of the word trust

explanation.surface: At last it is time to hand over the affairs of the trust.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark hours between dusk and dawn are a time of day.

clue.text: Pay me back nothing loaned without hesitation

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word me in reverse order

parts.note: nothing is zero, the round letter O

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the word for loaned wraps around the hesitation

parts.note: loaned means lent
um is the sound a speaker makes in hesitation

explanation.surface: A borrower is asked to repay money that was lent freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here is the old sense of outside, not the usual lacking, so the hesitation sits within the word for loaned.
explanation.definitionFit: An emolument is a salary or fee, the reward for work done.

clue.text: Rock music

definitions.meaning: to rock is to move back and forth
a style of big-band jazz from the 1930s

explanation.definitionFit: To sway to and fro is one sense; the other is the jazz style of Benny Goodman's big-band era.

clue.text: Head of the school — goody-goody youth

indicators.note: head of the school asks for the opening letter of the word school

parts.note: a prig is a smugly virtuous person

explanation.surface: A headteacher is dismissed as a sanctimonious young person.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shoot of a plant is used, in a dated way, for a young lad, a slip of a boy.

clue.text: Hint — it's altered and put back up a gum-tree

indicators.note: altered means the letters of the word hint are rearranged
put back means the synonym for the hint is written in reverse order

parts.note: it refers back to the hint, and a hint is a trace, a slight indication

explanation.surface: A suggestion is changed and then withdrawn, leaving someone stuck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altered' turns HINT into INTH; 'it' points back to the hint as TRACE, which 'put back' turns into ECART. 'In the cart' and 'up a gum-tree' are both British slang for in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are informal British idioms for being in serious difficulty or a fix.

clue.text: Pat used revised, newer versions'

indicators.note: revised means the letters of pat used are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Pat has brought out improved editions of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh releases or revisions that bring something current.

clue.text: Hairy rogues and vagabonds, literally

indicators.note: vagabonds wander, and literally says it is the letters of rogues and themselves that roam

explanation.surface: A shaggy band of rascals and wanderers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy' is slang for frightening or risky. 'literally' tells you to rearrange the letters of 'rogues and' rather than seek a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairy is informal for risky or frightening, as in a hairy moment.

clue.text: Some foreigners are cross — I keep quiet

parts.note: to span is to cross, as a bridge does
sh is the command to keep quiet

explanation.surface: Some people from abroad get angry while I say nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Spain, taken collectively, are one nation of foreigners.

clue.text: With happy heart open a trunk route up, a Roman road

indicators.note: heart asks for the middle of the word happy, all but its first and last letters
in a down clue, up means the next pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to yawn is to gape or open wide, as a chasm does
the A1 is Britain's Great North Road, a trunk route, with the figure 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A cheerful traveller opens up a main route on the way to an ancient highway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart' takes APP from happy. In a down clue 'up' reverses YAWN plus A1 (read AI) to give IANWAY.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient highway from Rome to Brindisi, built by Appius Claudius.

clue.text: As this oil is spilt, it gives an unpleasant smell

indicators.note: spilt suggests the letters of as this oil are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: Spilling this oil releases a nasty odour.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical term for bad breath, a persistent foul odour from the mouth.

clue.text: A number take exercise — they say it helps climbing

parts.note: ten is a number

indicators.note: they say signals that the word for exercise is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: drill is military exercise or practice

explanation.surface: Several people are told to work out, reportedly to help with mountaineering.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin coiling stem by which a vine or pea grips a support as it climbs.

clue.text: King's caught the ball

indicators.note: caught means holding, so the king's name wraps around the word the

parts.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragic king

explanation.surface: The monarch took a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the ball is called the leather, from its stitched cover; 'caught' suggests a catch but means holding.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricketers call the ball the leather after the hide it is covered in.

clue.text: One representative, a retired lady, put on the jury

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
an MP is a Member of Parliament, an elected representative

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the lady's name is read backwards

parts.note: Lena is a woman's name

explanation.surface: One MP and an elderly woman are called for jury service.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol people as jurors; the spelling empanel is the commoner variant.

clue.text: It's irritating one reformed smoker

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: reformed means the letters of smoker are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A former smoker who has quit can be tiresome.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiresome and annoying, the adjective from the verb irk, to annoy.

clue.text: Fellow holding the two of hearts, a card that's inferior

indicators.note: holding means the word for fellow keeps the next letter inside it

parts.note: a chap is a fellow

indicators.note: the two of picks out the second letter of the word hearts

parts.note: a jack is a court card

explanation.surface: A man with a low playing card and another card reckons his hand is poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the two of hearts' looks like a playing card but means the second letter of 'hearts', E.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap-jack describes goods of shoddy, inferior quality, as sold by a pedlar.

clue.text: Chap needs the right insurance

parts.note: cove is old British slang for a chap
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A man needs the correct insurance policy.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurance policies give protection against loss, which is the sense here.

clue.text: In the afternoon, little girl gives us a song

indicators.note: in means the little girl is placed inside the abbreviation for afternoon

parts.note: PM, post meridiem, is the afternoon
Sal is a short form of the girl's name Sally

explanation.surface: In the afternoon a young girl sings for us.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacred song or hymn, like those of the Old Testament book.

clue.text: Raised the roof over this

definitions.meaning: lifted high, up in the air
an attic space lies directly beneath the roof, so the roof is over it

explanation.definitionFit: Up high overhead, and, split in two, an attic room which has the roof directly over it.

clue.text: He has a point, accepted by someone outstanding

indicators.note: accepted by means the point is taken inside the word for someone outstanding

parts.note: a oner is British slang for a remarkable person
W, west, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A man has a valid argument, which an exceptional person agrees with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He has' is a cryptic description: the possessor of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A possessor is someone who holds something as his property.

clue.text: Shakespearian role — you can play it

definitions.meaning: the heroine of Twelfth Night, who disguises herself as Cesario
a stringed instrument, slightly larger than a violin

explanation.definitionFit: The shipwrecked heroine of Twelfth Night, and a bowed string instrument pitched below the violin.

clue.text: Robin joins bats and gulls

parts.note: Robin Hood, the legendary outlaw of Sherwood Forest
to bat an eyelid is to wink, so bats means winks

explanation.surface: The outlaw teams up with flying mammals and seabirds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bats' and 'gulls' look like animals; one is a verb for blinking, the other the definition, a verb meaning dupes.
explanation.definitionFit: To gull someone is to trick or deceive them.

clue.text: Show girls

parts.note: Rose is a girl's name
Marie is another girl's name

explanation.definitionFit: A 1924 musical set in the Canadian Rockies, later filmed with Nelson Eddy and Jeanette MacDonald.

clue.text: Battle of the century — Prestonpans

indicators.note: of the signals that the letters come from within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Prestonpans is billed as the great Scottish fight of the hundred years.
explanation.walkthrough: Prestonpans was a 1745 Jacobite battle in Scotland, so the surface reads as one battle; the answer is a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: A Belgian town that gave its name to three major First World War battles.
